newsitem.title: CROATIA: Bosnian Croat suspect to leave for Hague on Tuesday.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Croat suspect to leave for Hague on Tuesday.

text.p: Croatian authorities are holding indicted Bosnian Croat war crimes suspect Pero Skopljak in a Zagreb jail and are likely to transfer him to The Hague on Tuesday, court sources told Reuters on Monday.
The suspect will probably be flown out of Zagreb and taken to the International Criminal Tribunal for former Yugoslavia in the Dutch city at midday local time on Tuesday, the sources said.

"I know that one (Bosnian Croat) is here but I cannot give you the name or anything else," a judge at the Zagreb county court said on Monday. He added there were still legal proceedings to go through before Skopljak could be transferred.
Other court employees later told Reuters Skopljak was being held at Remetinec jail in a Zagreb suburb.
There was no information about whether Skopljak had handed himself into the authorities or whether he had been arrested.

The tribunal indicted Skopljak in November 1995 for persecuting Bosnian Moslems on political, racial and religious grounds between May 1992 and May 1993. He was indicted along with Dario Kordic, the most wanted Bosnian Croat war crimes suspect, and four others.

Skopljak was chief of police in the central Bosnian town of Vitez between October 1992 and May 1993. He and the other accused are said by the tribunal to have "effectively destroyed or removed almost the entire Moslem civilian population" of the Lasva Valley in Central Bosnia.
They are alleged to have imprisoned Moslem civilians, tortured them, used them as human shields and forced labour and murdered or otherwise killed some of the detainees.

Skopljak's detention comes amid intense international pressure on the former warring factions in ex-Yugoslavia to turn over war crimes suspects to the Hague tribunal -- the first international body for the prosecution of war crimes since the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials held after World War Two.
Foreign envoys have repeatedly told Croatian President Franjo Tudjman that they expect him to use his influence over Bosnian Croats to get them to hand over indictees.

Foreign Minister Mate Granic told his German counterpart Klaus Kinkel in Frankfurt on Saturday that seven indicted Bosnian Croats were ready to give themselves up to the tribunal if they were assured of a quick trial.

Many suspects are still seen to be influencing events in Bosnia, hampering the return of refugees to pre-war homes and pulling political strings from their hideouts. The two highest-profile suspects, former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic and general Ratko Mladic are still at large.

The United States is keen for its troops, serving in a NATO-led peace force in Bosnia, to leave by June 30, 1998 but politicians fear Bosnia will not be stable enough by then to allow them to withdraw.

Last month British forces arrested one Bosnian Serb indictee and shot dead a second who resisted arrest. Diplomats suggested what many war crimes suspects fear -- that the action could be a precursor to further swoops by NATO troops. So far, however, there has been no follow-up operation.
